subject: Agriculture
title: Herbicide-Resistant Crops
description: Learn Herbicide-Resistant Crops in one minute.

hook.text: Roundup Ready crops can survive glyphosate herbicide while weeds around them die. Monsanto built an empire on this.

buildup.text: Farmers plant Roundup Ready soybeans, spray glyphosate, and every weed dies. One chemical, total weed control.

discovery.text: By 2012, over 90% of US soybeans were Roundup Ready. Glyphosate use increased 15-fold in two decades.

twist.text: At least 50 weed species evolved glyphosate resistance. Superweeds now require multiple chemicals or hand weeding.

climax.text: The simplicity that made Roundup Ready popular also made resistance inevitable. Biology always adapts.

punchline.text: One herbicide, zero weeds—until the weeds evolved. Now: more herbicides, more problems.

quiz.question: What happened after decades of heavy glyphosate use on Roundup Ready crops?
options: At least 50 weed species evolved glyphosate resistance

details.summary: Herbicide-resistant crops are genetically engineered to survive application of specific herbicides, allowing farmers to spray weeds without damaging the crop. This topic covers the Roundup Ready revolution, the rise of superweeds, and the escalating arms race between chemistry and evolution.
details.whyItMatters: Herbicide-resistant crops transformed weed management but created a crisis of resistant superweeds now affecting over 100 million hectares. This arms race illustrates the limits of single-tactic pest management.
takeaways: Roundup Ready crops dominate U.S. soybean, corn, and cotton production since 1996
Over 260 weed species have now evolved resistance to one or more herbicides
Superweeds force farmers to use older, more toxic herbicides or return to tillage

faq.question: How do herbicide-resistant crops work?
faq.answer: Crops like Roundup Ready soybeans contain a gene that makes them immune to the herbicide glyphosate. Farmers spray the entire field, killing weeds while the crop survives. This simplified weed management and reduced tillage, but heavy herbicide use selected for resistant weeds.

faq.question: Why have superweeds become such a serious agricultural problem?
faq.answer: Repeated exposure to the same herbicide selects for naturally resistant weed individuals. These resistant weeds spread rapidly—Palmer amaranth can grow 2 inches per day and produce 600,000 seeds per plant. Farmers now face weeds immune to multiple herbicide classes simultaneously.
